meta.title: Vazira Ganesh
meta.foundedNote: The icon has an undated devotional origin tradition. Indian Express (2016) dates the governing trust to 1970; Sakal (2023) says 1974. Neither is treated here as the age of the rock-carved icon.
meta.intro: Vazira Ganesh is a permanent rock-carved shrine in Borivali West, also described as Swayambhu Shri Ganesh Mandir. The surrounding village, pond and temple complex are part of its history. Local accounts connect its development with Koli and Somvanshi Kshatriya Pathare residents. Its emergence is told through a quarry worker's dream; the tradition is recorded here as belief, while the precise age of the carving and the governing trust's establishment remain open questions.

paragraphs.text: The Ganesh image is carved into a large natural rock. Pudhari locates the complex inside Vazira village off Lokmanya Tilak Road, with a pond and the village deity Alji Dev nearby. Its account credits Koli and Somvanshi Kshatriya Pathare villagers with preparing and improving the site. The quarry worker's dream explains its sacred origin in local tradition; assertions of Pandava or Dravidian antiquity are not independently dated evidence.

In Srinath Rao's 2016 report, founding trustee Vishwas Rawte recalled cleaning the lake and beginning a permanent structure with friends in 1962. The report dates the governing trust to 1970. Sakal later gives 1974 for Shri Ganesh Gramstha Seva Mandal. These may concern different administrative stages, but no registration record was located to resolve them.

Sakal describes the seated, left-trunked icon and records chairman Vijaykumar Rawte's account that J. J. School of Art students removed accumulated vermilion in 1988, revealing its form. That retrospective testimony does not date the original carving. The article explicitly says the temple does not install a separate festival Ganesh; its January Ganesh Yag and local immersion pond belong to a continuing temple community.

Pudhari describes a hall, office, sheltered waiting area and garden around the shrine, alongside a gymnasium, free library, educational assistance and relief work. Such reporting documents the temple's wider role in village life. These are activities reported in 2025, rather than verified present-day service schedules or annual beneficiary totals.

sections.title: The village approach and an outdoor view of worship

paragraphs.text: In a 2014 first-person account, Arti identifies the shrine as Swayumbhu Siddhivinayak Ganesh Devasthan and describes approaching it through Vazira village. Her photographs show the festive village approach and the orange permanent Ganesh relief. The account also describes neighbouring shrines to Sheetla Mata and Hanuman. Its individual photographs are retained as undated views rather than assigned the publication year.

Arti's September 2015 festival essay dates its visit to immersion day, 27 September, and names this Borivli temple beside a photograph of an outdoor darshan screen. The screen displays the permanent rock icon for people outside. This is evidence of mediated access to worship during the festival, distinct from the temporary Ganesh figures brought for immersion; it does not show the rock icon being removed.

media.label: Outdoor darshan screen - 2015 festival visit
media.caption: A screen outside Vazira's named Ganesh temple displays the orange permanent rock icon during the 2015 immersion-day visit. This is a photograph of a screen, not a direct shrine portrait.
media.credit: Arti / My Yatra Diary; visible watermark retained.
media.yearConfidence: Contemporary first-person event report; no independent camera date.
media.dateEvidence: Essay published 29 September 2015 opens with 27 September, Ganesh Visarjan; caption next to this screen names the Swayumbhu Siddhivinayak temple in Borivli. The screen itself cannot establish capture date.

visualReview.observedForm: Outdoor LED screen beneath a dark canopy displays orange Ganesh relief in a rough rock surrounded by concentric flower bands. A tall orange Marathi banner alongside welcomes devotees to Swayambhu Shri Ganesh Devasthan; twilight sky and watermark visible.
visualReview.note: Native 800px photograph viewed. The photographed screen and temple-name banner support the local identification; the depicted year follows the contemporary event narrative.

researchNotes.coverage: Expanded research, 16 November 2026: added a contemporary 2015 named-temple e-darshan photograph and an undated village-approach view from a first-person local account. Six sources, three dated records and two undated media; trust-date conflict remains open.
